title: lilC C Programming Quizzes
description: Ten Swift-friendly C programming quizzes progressing from easy to hard, focused on undergraduate and job-ready syntax, semantics, debugging, and practical C reasoning.

quizzes.title: C Foundations: Declarations, Types, and Expressions

questions.title: Minimal hosted program
questions.prompt: Which definition is the standard hosted entry point for a simple C program?
questions.explanation: A hosted C program starts at main, and int main(void) is a clear standard-conforming form.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the conventional, portable shape of main.

questions.title: Declaration grammar
questions.prompt: Which line declares an integer variable named count and initializes it to 10?
questions.explanation: C declarations put the base type before the declarator, followed by an optional initializer.
questions.learningObjective: Read and write basic variable declarations.

questions.title: Header for printf
questions.prompt: Which header should be included before calling printf in portable C?
questions.explanation: printf is declared by stdio.h. Including it lets the compiler check the call.
questions.learningObjective: Know which standard header declares common I/O functions.

questions.title: Integer division
questions.prompt: What value is stored in x?
questions.explanation: Both operands are int, so / performs integer division and discards the fractional part.
questions.learningObjective: Understand how operand types affect arithmetic.

questions.title: Forgetting initialization
questions.prompt: What is true about reading n here?
choices: It contains the previous value assigned to any variable named n.
It has an indeterminate value; reading it is undefined behavior.
The compiler must reject the program.
questions.explanation: Automatic local variables are not initialized unless you initialize them. Reading an uninitialized int has undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid assuming local variables start with a useful value.

questions.title: Pointer declarator binding
questions.prompt: What does this declaration create?
choices: Both p and q are pointers to int.
p is an int, and q is a pointer to int.
p is a pointer to int, and q is an int.
questions.explanation: The * belongs to the declarator p, not to the base type shared by q.
questions.learningObjective: Read C declarators accurately.

questions.title: Character versus string literal
questions.prompt: Which expression has type int in C, even though it represents a character value?
questions.explanation: A character constant such as 'A' has type int in C. A string literal such as "A" is an array of char.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish character constants from string literals.

questions.title: sizeof an array
questions.prompt: On a system where int is 4 bytes, what is sizeof a?
choices: It depends on the values stored in a.
questions.explanation: sizeof applied to an actual array gives the total byte size: 5 elements times 4 bytes.
questions.learningObjective: Use sizeof correctly on objects with known type.

questions.title: Assignment inside condition
questions.prompt: What happens when this if statement runs?
choices: x is compared with 3, and the body executes only if x was already 3.
The compiler must reject assignment in an if condition.
x becomes 3, and the body executes.
x becomes 0, and the body is skipped.
questions.explanation: The expression x = 3 assigns 3 and evaluates to 3, which is true in C.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize assignment expressions and avoid confusing them with comparison.

questions.title: Equality operator
questions.prompt: Which operator tests whether two scalar values are equal?
questions.explanation: == compares values. = assigns a value.
questions.learningObjective: Choose comparison syntax correctly.

questions.title: Prefix increment
questions.prompt: After these statements, what are a and b?
questions.explanation: ++a increments first and then yields the new value.
questions.learningObjective: Understand prefix increment without introducing undefined behavior.

questions.title: Postfix increment
questions.prompt: After these statements, what are a and b?
questions.explanation: a++ yields the old value, then increments a.
questions.learningObjective: Understand postfix increment in simple expressions.

questions.title: Floating result
questions.prompt: Which expression computes 2.5 as a double?
questions.explanation: Casting one operand to double causes floating-point division.
questions.learningObjective: Use casts to control arithmetic conversions.

questions.title: Remainder operator
questions.prompt: What is printed?
choices: The code is invalid because % only works on unsigned integers.
questions.explanation: % gives the integer remainder. 10 divided by 3 leaves remainder 1.
questions.learningObjective: Use the remainder operator with integer operands.

questions.title: String terminator
questions.prompt: How many char elements are needed to store the string "cat" as a C string?
questions.explanation: A C string needs one extra null character, '\0', after the visible characters.
questions.learningObjective: Remember that C strings are null-terminated arrays of char.

questions.title: Valid identifier
questions.prompt: Which is a valid ordinary C identifier?
questions.explanation: Identifiers can contain letters, digits, and underscores, but cannot start with a digit or be a keyword.
questions.learningObjective: Apply C identifier naming rules.

questions.title: Block scope
questions.prompt: Which statement about x is correct?
choices: The code is invalid because x is declared twice anywhere in a function.
The inner x hides the outer x only inside the braces.
Both variables are visible everywhere in f.
questions.explanation: A declaration in an inner block can hide an outer declaration until that block ends.
questions.learningObjective: Understand block scope and name hiding.

questions.title: Escape sequence
questions.prompt: Which escape sequence represents a newline character in a C string literal?
questions.explanation: \n is the newline escape sequence used in C string and character literals.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize common escape sequences.

questions.title: Boolean conditions in C
questions.prompt: In an if condition, which value is considered false?
questions.explanation: In C, zero is false and any nonzero scalar value is true.
questions.learningObjective: Understand truth values in C control flow.

questions.title: Compilation unit basics
questions.prompt: What is a translation unit in C?
choices: A source file after preprocessing, compiled as one unit.
questions.explanation: The compiler compiles each preprocessed source file as a translation unit.
questions.learningObjective: Connect source files, preprocessing, and compilation.

questions.title: Short-circuit AND
questions.prompt: Why is this condition safe when p may be NULL?
choices: && evaluates both operands in random order.
*p is never evaluated in C conditions.
NULL can be dereferenced safely in conditions.
p is checked before *p is evaluated.
questions.explanation: && evaluates left to right and skips the right operand if the left operand is false.
questions.learningObjective: Use short-circuit operators to guard risky expressions.

questions.title: Short-circuit OR
questions.prompt: If ready is nonzero, what happens to start()?
choices: start() may or may not be called.
The expression is invalid unless ready is _Bool.
questions.explanation: || skips the right operand when the left operand is true.
questions.learningObjective: Predict evaluation of logical OR.

questions.title: Dangling else
questions.prompt: Which if does the else bind to?
choices: The nearest unmatched if, which is if (b).
questions.explanation: In C, else associates with the nearest previous if that does not already have an else.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid ambiguity by understanding else binding.

questions.title: Switch fallthrough
questions.prompt: What is printed when n is 1?
questions.explanation: Without break, execution falls through from case 1 into case 2.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize switch fallthrough and when break is needed.

questions.title: Continue in a for loop
questions.prompt: What does continue do in this loop?
choices: Skips i++ and repeats with the same i.
Skips the rest of the loop body, then performs i++ and tests the condition.
questions.explanation: In a for loop, continue proceeds to the iteration expression before testing the loop condition again.
questions.learningObjective: Understand continue behavior in for loops.

questions.title: break target
questions.prompt: Inside nested loops, what does break exit?
choices: Only the nearest enclosing loop or switch.
questions.explanation: break exits the closest enclosing loop or switch statement.
questions.learningObjective: Know the scope of break.

questions.title: do while timing
questions.prompt: How many times is the body guaranteed to run in a do while loop?
choices: Only if the condition is initially true.
questions.explanation: The condition is tested after the body, so the body runs before the first test.
questions.learningObjective: Choose the right loop form for post-test logic.

questions.title: for loop parts
questions.prompt: Which part of a for loop executes after each completed iteration body?
choices: The initializer, such as int i = 0.
The condition before the body finishes.
The iteration expression, such as i++.
questions.explanation: A for loop runs initializer once, then checks condition, body, and iteration expression repeatedly.
questions.learningObjective: Understand for-loop execution order.

questions.title: Operator precedence
questions.prompt: What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so 1 + (2 * 3) is 7.
questions.learningObjective: Apply basic operator precedence.

questions.title: Parentheses and intent
questions.prompt: What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Parentheses force addition before multiplication: (1 + 2) * 3.
questions.learningObjective: Use parentheses to express intended grouping.

questions.title: Logical NOT
questions.prompt: What value does !x produce when x is 0?
questions.explanation: ! yields 1 when its operand compares equal to zero, otherwise 0.
questions.learningObjective: Understand the result of logical negation.

questions.title: Relational result
questions.prompt: What is stored in b?
questions.explanation: Relational operators produce int value 1 for true and 0 for false.
questions.learningObjective: Understand that comparisons produce integer truth values.

questions.title: Comma operator
questions.prompt: What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: The comma operator evaluates the left expression, discards it, then yields the right expression.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the comma operator and avoid confusing it with argument separators.

questions.title: Conditional operator
questions.prompt: What is assigned to max?
choices: The larger of a and b.
The smaller of a and b.
questions.explanation: The ?: operator selects the second expression when the condition is true, otherwise the third.
questions.learningObjective: Use the conditional operator for simple selection.

questions.title: Loop off by one
questions.prompt: For an array of length len, which loop visits valid indexes from 0 through len - 1?
questions.explanation: The valid indexes are less than len. Using <= len visits one past the end.
questions.learningObjective: Write correct bounds for array loops.

questions.title: Empty statement trap
questions.prompt: What is the bug in this code?
choices: The braces are illegal after a for loop.
The semicolon makes the for loop body empty.
printf cannot be called inside braces.
questions.explanation: The semicolon immediately after the for statement is an empty loop body. The block runs once after the loop.
questions.learningObjective: Spot accidental empty statements after control headers.

questions.title: switch expression type
questions.prompt: Which kind of expression can be used as a switch controlling expression?
questions.explanation: switch works with integer types, including char and enum values.
questions.learningObjective: Know the type restrictions of switch.

questions.title: case label requirement
questions.prompt: What must a case label be?
choices: Any variable that currently has an integer value.
questions.explanation: case labels are compile-time integer constant expressions.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish compile-time case labels from runtime values.

questions.title: while versus if
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between while (condition) and if (condition)?
choices: if can repeat the body; while cannot.
while can repeat the body; if executes it at most once.
while requires braces; if does not.
questions.explanation: while rechecks the condition after each body execution, allowing repetition.
questions.learningObjective: Choose appropriate control-flow statements.

questions.title: Return from non-void function
questions.prompt: What should a non-void function normally do on every reachable path?
choices: Declare at least one local variable.
Return a value of a compatible type.
questions.explanation: A non-void function is expected to return a value. Falling off the end can lead to undefined behavior when the caller uses the result.
questions.learningObjective: Understand return requirements for functions.

questions.title: Array first index
questions.prompt: What is the index of the first element in a C array?
choices: It depends on the array length.
questions.explanation: C arrays use zero-based indexing.
questions.learningObjective: Use correct array indexes.

questions.title: Array initializer size
questions.prompt: How many elements does a have?
choices: The declaration is invalid without an explicit size.
questions.explanation: When the size is omitted, the initializer determines the number of elements.
questions.learningObjective: Infer array sizes from initializers.

questions.title: Partially initialized array
questions.prompt: What is a[3] after this initialization?
questions.explanation: Missing elements in an aggregate initializer are initialized to zero.
questions.learningObjective: Understand partial aggregate initialization.

questions.title: Array bounds
questions.prompt: For int a[3], which index is one past the last valid element?
questions.explanation: Valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2. Index 3 is one past the array and must not be dereferenced.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid off-by-one array access.

questions.title: String literal storage
questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
choices: It attempts to modify a string literal, which has undefined behavior.
char * cannot point to a string literal.
The string has no null terminator.
Only the second character can be modified.
questions.explanation: String literals should be treated as read-only; modifying one has undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid writing through pointers to string literals.

questions.title: Modifiable string array
questions.prompt: Which declaration creates a modifiable array containing the characters h, i, and '\0'?
questions.explanation: char s[] initializes an array object with a copy of the string literal's characters.
questions.learningObjective: Choose between string arrays and string-literal pointers.

questions.title: strlen result
questions.prompt: What does strlen("abc") return?
choices: The number of bytes allocated by the compiler for the literal.
questions.explanation: strlen counts characters before the terminating null character, not the terminator itself.
questions.learningObjective: Understand C string length.

questions.title: Header for strlen
questions.prompt: Which header declares strlen?
questions.explanation: strlen and many other string functions are declared in string.h.
questions.learningObjective: Know standard headers for string functions.

questions.title: Function prototype
questions.prompt: Which is a valid prototype for a function that takes two ints and returns int?
questions.explanation: A prototype specifies the return type, function name, and parameter types.
questions.learningObjective: Write function declarations that enable call checking.

questions.title: Pass by value
questions.prompt: What is printed?
questions.explanation: C passes int arguments by value. Changing x inside bump does not change n in main.
questions.learningObjective: Understand pass-by-value for scalar parameters.

questions.title: Changing caller variable
questions.prompt: Which function can change the caller's int variable?
questions.explanation: Passing a pointer lets the function write to the caller's object through indirection.
questions.learningObjective: Use pointers when a function must update a caller-owned object.

questions.title: Array parameter adjustment
questions.prompt: Inside f, what is the type of a after parameter adjustment?
questions.explanation: Array parameters are adjusted to pointer parameters. The 10 is not preserved as part of the parameter type.
questions.learningObjective: Understand array-to-pointer adjustment in function parameters.

questions.title: Need length with array parameter
questions.prompt: Why should this function also receive the array length?
choices: sizeof a gives the size of a pointer, not the original array.
C arrays always store their length at index -1.
The compiler forbids loops over array parameters.
The length can be recovered with strlen for any array.
questions.explanation: In a function parameter, a is a pointer, so sizeof a cannot tell how many elements the caller's array had.
questions.learningObjective: Pass array lengths explicitly when needed.

questions.title: Return local address
questions.prompt: What is wrong with this function?
choices: It returns an int instead of a pointer.
It returns the address of a local variable whose lifetime ends when the function returns.
The & operator cannot be used on int variables.
questions.explanation: The local variable x stops existing after bad returns, so the returned pointer is dangling.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid returning pointers to automatic local objects.

questions.title: static local lifetime
questions.prompt: What is true about count?
choices: It is recreated and uninitialized on every call.
It is initialized once and retains its value between calls.
It can only store constant values.
questions.explanation: A static local variable has block scope but static storage duration.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish scope from storage duration.

questions.title: void parameter list
questions.prompt: In a function declaration, what does int f(void); mean?
choices: f takes an unspecified number of arguments.
questions.explanation: void in the parameter list explicitly means no parameters.
questions.learningObjective: Write no-argument function prototypes correctly.

questions.title: Return type void
questions.prompt: Which statement is valid inside a void function?
questions.explanation: A void function may use return; to exit without producing a value.
questions.learningObjective: Use return correctly in void functions.

questions.title: Prototype mismatch
questions.prompt: Why is a visible prototype helpful before a function call?
choices: It causes the function to run faster automatically.
It lets the compiler check argument count and types.
It stores the function body in the header.
questions.explanation: A prototype tells the compiler the function interface before calls are compiled.
questions.learningObjective: Use prototypes to catch call mistakes early.

questions.title: String copy destination
questions.prompt: What must be true before strcpy(dst, src) is safe?
choices: src must be shorter than 5 characters.
dst may be a string literal.
dst must point to enough writable storage for src and its null terminator.
The two pointers must have the same address.
questions.explanation: strcpy does not allocate space or check the destination size.
questions.learningObjective: Respect storage requirements for C string operations.

questions.title: Null character in strings
questions.prompt: What does '\0' usually mark in a C string?
choices: A character that prints as zero.
questions.explanation: C string functions stop at the first null character.
questions.learningObjective: Understand null termination.

questions.title: Address operator
questions.prompt: What does &x produce?
choices: A copy of x as a string.
questions.explanation: The unary & operator yields a pointer to its operand.
questions.learningObjective: Use the address-of operator correctly.

questions.title: Indirection operator
questions.prompt: What does *p mean when p is an int * pointing at a valid int?
choices: The address stored in p as an integer.
The number of bytes in p.
The int object that p points to.
A declaration only, never an expression.
questions.explanation: In an expression, *p dereferences the pointer and accesses the pointed-to int.
questions.learningObjective: Understand pointer indirection in expressions.

questions.title: Pointer initialization
questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
choices: All int pointers automatically point to zero.
p is uninitialized, so dereferencing it has undefined behavior.
questions.explanation: A pointer must hold a valid address before you use *p to read or write.
questions.learningObjective: Initialize pointers before dereferencing them.

questions.title: NULL check
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of checking p != NULL before *p?
choices: To avoid dereferencing a null pointer.
To convert p to an int.
To make p point to zero.
questions.explanation: Dereferencing a null pointer has undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Guard pointer dereferences.

questions.title: Pointer arithmetic scale
questions.prompt: If p points to a[0], what does p + 2 point to?
choices: The address two bytes after a[0]
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type.
questions.learningObjective: Understand how pointer arithmetic relates to array elements.

questions.title: Array decay
questions.prompt: In most expressions, what does the array name a convert to?
choices: A pointer to the whole array object.
A pointer to its first element.
questions.explanation: Except in contexts such as sizeof, unary &, and string literal initialization, an array expression converts to a pointer to its first element.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize array-to-pointer conversion.

questions.title: Pointer to whole array
questions.prompt: What is the type of p?
choices: Pointer to an array of 5 int.
questions.explanation: Parentheses make p a pointer to the whole array type int[5].
questions.learningObjective: Read pointer-to-array declarations.

questions.title: Array of pointers
questions.prompt: What does this declaration create?
choices: An array of 3 pointers to int.
A pointer to an array of 3 int.
A pointer to a function returning int.
questions.explanation: The brackets bind to p, so p is an array; each element is int *.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish arrays of pointers from pointers to arrays.

questions.title: const pointer target
questions.prompt: What does const int *p mean?
choices: p itself cannot be changed to point elsewhere.
p points to an int that should not be modified through p.
p points to a const pointer.
questions.explanation: const applies to the pointed-to int. The pointer variable p may still be assigned another address.
questions.learningObjective: Read const-qualified pointer declarations.

questions.title: const pointer variable
questions.prompt: What does int * const p mean?
choices: p points to a constant int.
p is a pointer to a pointer.
p is a constant pointer to int.
p is an array of const int.
questions.explanation: const after * qualifies the pointer object itself, so p cannot be reassigned after initialization.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish pointer constness from pointed-to constness.

questions.title: Double pointer use
questions.prompt: Why might a function take int **out?
choices: To modify only a local int value.
To return two int values automatically.
To make pointer arithmetic twice as fast.
To modify the caller's int * variable.
questions.explanation: A pointer to pointer lets the function write a new pointer value into the caller's pointer variable.
questions.learningObjective: Understand when pointer-to-pointer parameters are useful.

questions.title: Dangling pointer after scope
questions.prompt: What is p after the block ends?
choices: A dangling pointer; using *p is undefined behavior.
A valid pointer to x forever.
A pointer automatically redirected to a copy of x.
questions.explanation: x has automatic storage duration and stops existing when the block exits.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid pointers to expired local objects.

questions.title: Pointer comparison
questions.prompt: Which comparison is well-defined?
choices: Comparing two pointers into the same array with <.
Comparing any two function pointers with <.
Comparing a pointer with an integer using < to sort addresses portably.
questions.explanation: Relational pointer comparisons are defined for pointers into the same array object or one past it.
questions.learningObjective: Know the limits of pointer ordering comparisons.

questions.title: One-past pointer
questions.prompt: What can you do with a one-past-the-end pointer?
choices: Dereference it to get the last element.
Use it as a valid place to write one extra element.
Compare it or subtract it within the same array, but not dereference it.
questions.explanation: C permits forming one-past pointers for array traversal, but dereferencing them is undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Use sentinel pointers safely.

questions.title: Pointer subtraction
questions.prompt: When is p - q defined?
choices: Only when p and q point to equal values.
When p and q point into the same array object or one past it.
questions.explanation: Pointer subtraction is defined only within one array object and yields an element count.
questions.learningObjective: Apply pointer arithmetic rules correctly.

questions.title: void pointer
questions.prompt: What is a common use of void *?
choices: Holding a generic object pointer that must be converted before dereference.
Storing an int value without memory.
Dereferencing objects without knowing their type.
questions.explanation: void * can hold object pointers, but you need an object type to access the pointed-to storage.
questions.learningObjective: Use generic object pointers safely.

questions.title: Pointer format
questions.prompt: Which printf conversion should be used for a pointer value after casting to void *?
questions.explanation: %p prints a pointer value; the argument should be converted to void *.
questions.learningObjective: Print pointer values correctly for debugging.

questions.title: Out parameter pattern
questions.prompt: Which call matches void read_value(int *out)?
questions.explanation: The function expects the address of an int it can write through.
questions.learningObjective: Pass addresses to pointer parameters intentionally.

questions.title: Pointer and array notation
questions.prompt: For a valid pointer p, what is p[i] equivalent to?
questions.explanation: The subscript operator is defined in terms of pointer addition and indirection.
questions.learningObjective: Connect array indexing to pointer arithmetic.

questions.title: Dereference before assignment
questions.prompt: Which statement changes the int object pointed to by p?
questions.explanation: *p designates the pointed-to int. Assigning to p itself would change the pointer value.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish changing a pointer from changing the object it points to.

quizzes.title: Scope, Storage Duration, and Multi-File Interfaces

questions.title: File-scope static
questions.prompt: What does static mean at file scope?
choices: The variable is stored on the stack.
The name has internal linkage and is visible only within that translation unit.
The variable is initialized every time a function is called.
questions.explanation: At file scope, static gives a name internal linkage, hiding it from other translation units.
questions.learningObjective: Use static to limit file-scope visibility.

questions.title: extern declaration
questions.prompt: What does this declaration usually mean in a header?
choices: counter is defined separately in every file that includes the header.
counter is local to each function.
counter is defined in exactly one source file elsewhere.
questions.explanation: extern declares an object with external linkage without defining storage for it.
questions.learningObjective: Separate declarations from definitions across files.

questions.title: Header variable mistake
questions.prompt: Why is defining int counter; in a header risky?
choices: Each including source file may define its own counter, causing multiple-definition link errors.
questions.explanation: A header included by several .c files can produce several definitions of the same external object.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid defining external objects in headers.

questions.title: Include guard purpose
questions.prompt: What problem do include guards prevent?
choices: Linker errors from missing object files.
Repeated inclusion of the same header's contents in one translation unit.
questions.explanation: Include guards use macros to make a header's declarations appear only once per translation unit.
questions.learningObjective: Use include guards to protect headers.

questions.title: Function declaration versus definition
questions.prompt: Which line is a function declaration but not a definition?
choices: int sum(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
questions.explanation: The semicolon form declares the interface without providing a function body.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish prototypes from function bodies.

questions.title: Global initialization
questions.prompt: What is the initial value of file-scope int total if no initializer is provided?
questions.explanation: Objects with static storage duration are initialized to zero before program startup.
questions.learningObjective: Know default initialization for static storage duration.

questions.title: Automatic initialization
questions.prompt: What is the initial value of block-scope int total without an initializer?
questions.explanation: Automatic local variables are not zero-initialized by default.
questions.learningObjective: Do not rely on default values for automatic locals.

questions.title: Lifetime of static local
questions.prompt: How long does a static local variable exist?
choices: For the entire execution of the program.
Only until the function returns the first time.
questions.explanation: A static local has static storage duration even though its name has block scope.
questions.learningObjective: Separate lifetime from name visibility.

questions.title: Prototype in header
questions.prompt: What should usually go in a header for a function used by multiple .c files?
choices: The same non-static function definition copied into every source file.
All local variables used by the function.
A prototype such as int parse(const char *s);
questions.explanation: Headers should expose declarations needed by users of the module.
questions.learningObjective: Design clean C interfaces.

questions.title: static function
questions.prompt: Why declare a helper function static in a .c file?
choices: To make it remember local variables automatically.
To prevent it from being called recursively.
To give it internal linkage so it cannot conflict with functions in other files.
questions.explanation: static at file scope limits the function name to one translation unit.
questions.learningObjective: Use internal linkage for private helpers.

questions.title: Name hiding
questions.prompt: What does this function print?
questions.explanation: The block-scope x hides the file-scope x inside f.
questions.learningObjective: Track which declaration a name refers to.

questions.title: Register keyword reality
questions.prompt: What is a practical modern view of register?
choices: It guarantees the variable is stored in a CPU register.
It is mostly obsolete; compilers usually choose register allocation themselves.
It gives the name external linkage.
questions.explanation: register is a hint with restrictions, not a guarantee, and modern optimizers rarely need it.
questions.learningObjective: Understand storage-class specifiers without overtrusting them.

questions.title: Linker unresolved symbol
questions.prompt: A compiler accepts a call to helper(), but the linker reports an undefined reference to helper. What is the likely issue?
choices: The function has too many local variables.
The function returned the wrong value at runtime.
No linked object file provides the function definition.
The preprocessor expanded helper incorrectly in every case.
questions.explanation: The compiler can compile a call from a declaration, but the linker must find exactly one external definition.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish compile-time declarations from link-time definitions.

questions.title: Multiple definition
questions.prompt: What commonly causes a multiple definition linker error?
choices: Declaring a function prototype in a header.
Defining the same external function or object in more than one translation unit.
questions.explanation: External names must have compatible declarations and normally one definition across the linked program.
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose common linker errors.

questions.title: Header self-sufficiency
questions.prompt: What does it mean for a header to be self-sufficient?
choices: It can be included by itself because it includes or forward-declares what it needs.
It contains every function body in the program.
It only works when included last.
questions.explanation: A good header should not require users to include some other header first by accident.
questions.learningObjective: Design robust C headers.

questions.title: Forward declaration of struct
questions.prompt: Which declaration can hide the fields of struct Node while allowing pointers to it?
questions.explanation: An incomplete struct declaration allows pointer declarations without exposing the definition.
questions.learningObjective: Use opaque structs in interfaces.

questions.title: Inline in headers
questions.prompt: Why can non-static function definitions in headers be a problem?
choices: Every including source file may define the same external function.
They prevent include guards from working.
questions.explanation: Include guards prevent repeated inclusion within one translation unit, not definitions across several translation units.
questions.learningObjective: Understand why headers usually contain declarations, not external definitions.

questions.title: Local static initialization
questions.prompt: When is this static local initialized?
choices: Only if f is declared in a header.
Before program startup or before first use, according to C initialization rules for static storage duration.
questions.explanation: A static local has static storage duration and is not reinitialized on each call.
questions.learningObjective: Predict initialization behavior for static locals.

questions.title: extern function default
questions.prompt: What linkage do non-static file-scope function definitions have by default?
questions.explanation: A normal file-scope function definition is externally visible unless declared static.
questions.learningObjective: Know default linkage for functions.

questions.title: Header includes implementation header
questions.prompt: What is the best reason not to put private implementation details in a public header?
choices: The preprocessor cannot process private names.
It exposes internals and forces users to recompile when private details change.
Public headers cannot include standard headers.
questions.explanation: Keeping public headers small reduces coupling and makes modules easier to maintain.
questions.learningObjective: Separate public interfaces from implementation details.

questions.title: Struct member access
questions.prompt: Which expression accesses member x of a struct Point variable p?
questions.explanation: The . operator accesses a member through a struct object.
questions.learningObjective: Use struct member access syntax.

questions.title: Pointer member access
questions.prompt: Which expression accesses member x through a struct Point *p?
questions.explanation: p->x is shorthand for (*p).x.
questions.learningObjective: Use arrow syntax for pointers to structs.

questions.title: Struct assignment
questions.prompt: What does b = a do for two variables of the same struct type?
choices: Copies the whole struct object member-by-member.
questions.explanation: C supports assignment between compatible struct objects; pointer members are copied as pointer values.
questions.learningObjective: Understand struct assignment behavior.

questions.title: Designated initializer
questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of this initializer?
choices: It initializes fields in random order at runtime.
It names the fields being initialized.
It prevents zero-initialization of missing fields.
questions.explanation: Designators make initialization clearer and less dependent on member order.
questions.learningObjective: Use designated initializers for readable aggregate setup.

questions.title: Missing struct initializer fields
questions.prompt: What happens to omitted members in an aggregate initializer?
choices: The compiler must reject the initializer.
They copy values from the previous struct object.
They are initialized as if they had static zero initialization.
questions.explanation: Omitted aggregate members are initialized to zero/null-equivalent values.
questions.learningObjective: Predict aggregate initialization results.

questions.title: Typedef alias
questions.prompt: What does this typedef create?
choices: Point as an alias for struct Point.
questions.explanation: typedef introduces an alias name for an existing type.
questions.learningObjective: Use typedefs to name struct types conveniently.

questions.title: Anonymous struct typedef
questions.prompt: After this declaration, which type name can you use?
questions.explanation: The struct has no tag, but the typedef name Point can name the type.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize typedef names versus struct tags.

questions.title: Enum default values
questions.prompt: What are the values of RED, GREEN, and BLUE?
questions.explanation: Unassigned enum constants start at 0 and increase by 1.
questions.learningObjective: Use enum constants predictably.

questions.title: Enum explicit values
questions.prompt: What is the value of C?
questions.explanation: After B is explicitly 5, the next enumerator C becomes 6.
questions.learningObjective: Track enum value assignment.

questions.title: Union storage
questions.prompt: What is the key property of a union?
choices: All members share the same storage.
All members are stored independently like a struct.
It cannot be passed to functions.
questions.explanation: A union overlays its members in one storage area, so only one member value is intended to be active at a time.
questions.learningObjective: Understand union memory layout at a practical level.

questions.title: Union overwrite
questions.prompt: What happens conceptually after assigning u.i and then u.f?
choices: The shared storage now holds the f member's representation.
The assignment to f is ignored.
The code must fail to compile.
questions.explanation: Union members share storage, so writing one member overwrites the bytes used by the other.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid assuming unions store all members simultaneously.

questions.title: Struct padding
questions.prompt: Why might sizeof(struct S) be larger than sizeof(char) + sizeof(int)?
questions.codeSnippet: struct S { char c; int x; };
choices: char members are stored as int.
The compiler may add padding for alignment.
questions.explanation: Compilers insert padding so members meet alignment requirements.
questions.learningObjective: Account for padding when reasoning about struct size.

questions.title: Nested struct access
questions.prompt: Which expression accesses rect.origin.x when rect is a struct object?
questions.explanation: Use . at each level when each intermediate value is a struct object.
questions.learningObjective: Access nested struct members correctly.

questions.title: Struct pointer parameter
questions.prompt: Why pass a large struct as const struct Config *cfg?
choices: To avoid copying it while promising not to modify it through cfg.
To force it onto the heap.
To make all members compile-time constants.
To allow cfg to be used after the caller returns.
questions.explanation: A pointer avoids copying, and const documents/enforces read-only access through that pointer.
questions.learningObjective: Choose efficient and clear struct function parameters.

questions.title: Self-referential struct
questions.prompt: Which member can be used for a linked-list node pointing to the next node?
questions.explanation: A struct cannot contain a complete instance of itself, but it can contain a pointer to the same struct type.
questions.learningObjective: Declare self-referential structures correctly.

questions.title: Flexible array member
questions.prompt: What is true about a flexible array member such as char data[] at the end of a struct?
choices: It can appear as the first member.
Extra storage can be allocated after the struct object for the array elements.
sizeof includes space for 100 elements by default.
questions.explanation: A flexible array member has no fixed size in sizeof the struct and is used with dynamically allocated extra storage.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize the purpose and placement of flexible array members.

questions.title: Typedef pointer trap
questions.prompt: Given typedef int *IntPtr; what does this declare?
choices: a is a pointer, b is an int.
a is an int, b is a pointer.
The typedef is ignored in declarations.
Both a and b are pointers to int.
questions.explanation: The typedef name IntPtr already includes the pointer declarator, so each declared object has that alias type.
questions.learningObjective: Read typedef-based pointer declarations carefully.

questions.title: Struct tag namespace
questions.prompt: In C, what is true about struct tags and ordinary identifiers?
choices: They are in different name spaces.
They must always have different spelling.
A struct tag automatically creates a typedef.
Tags can only be used inside functions.
questions.explanation: C keeps tags such as struct Point separate from ordinary identifiers and typedef names.
questions.learningObjective: Understand C's distinct name spaces.

questions.title: Passing struct by value
questions.prompt: If a function receives struct Point p by value and changes p.x, what happens to the caller's struct?
questions.explanation: The parameter is a copy of the caller's struct object.
questions.learningObjective: Understand value semantics for struct parameters.

questions.title: Enum use case
questions.prompt: Why use an enum for states such as TOKEN_INT, TOKEN_NAME, TOKEN_END?
choices: It prevents all invalid values at runtime.
It gives readable named integer constants for a closed set of states.
It creates separate variables for every state.
questions.explanation: Enums make related integer constants clearer, though C may still allow out-of-range values in enum objects.
questions.learningObjective: Use enums for readable state sets.

questions.title: malloc header
questions.prompt: Which header declares malloc, calloc, realloc, and free?
questions.explanation: The standard memory allocation functions are declared in stdlib.h.
questions.learningObjective: Include the correct header for allocation functions.

questions.title: malloc failure
questions.prompt: What can malloc return when allocation fails?
choices: A pointer that should still be freed twice
questions.explanation: malloc returns a null pointer on failure.
questions.learningObjective: Handle allocation failure safely.

questions.title: Correct allocation size
questions.prompt: Which allocation is usually safest for an array of n int objects?
questions.explanation: sizeof *a follows the pointed-to type and avoids accidentally using the pointer size.
questions.learningObjective: Allocate the right number of bytes for arrays.

questions.title: calloc behavior
questions.prompt: What does calloc(n, sizeof *p) do that malloc(n * sizeof *p) does not?
choices: Initializes all bytes of the allocated storage to zero.
questions.explanation: calloc zero-initializes the allocated storage if allocation succeeds.
questions.learningObjective: Know the difference between malloc and calloc.

questions.title: free null
questions.prompt: What happens when free(NULL) is called?
choices: Nothing; it is defined to be safe.
questions.explanation: The C standard defines free(NULL) as a no-op.
questions.learningObjective: Use cleanup code without unnecessary NULL special cases.

questions.title: Double free
questions.prompt: What is wrong with freeing the same allocated pointer twice?
choices: It is required to be ignored.
It resets the pointer to NULL automatically.
questions.explanation: After free(p), the allocation is no longer owned; freeing it again is undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid double-free bugs.

questions.title: Use after free
questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
choices: free requires the size as a second argument.
The first assignment must use memcpy.
The code writes through p after its allocation has been freed.
malloc returns initialized memory only for int.
questions.explanation: Accessing storage after it has been freed is undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid use-after-free bugs.

questions.title: realloc failure pattern
questions.prompt: Why is assigning realloc directly to p risky?
choices: realloc always frees p before trying to allocate.
realloc returns an int, not a pointer.
If realloc fails, the original allocation is still allocated but p is overwritten with NULL.
questions.explanation: Use a temporary pointer so you do not lose the only reference to the original allocation on failure.
questions.learningObjective: Handle realloc failures without leaking memory.

questions.title: String allocation length
questions.prompt: How many bytes should be allocated to copy a string of length len?
questions.explanation: You need one extra byte for the terminating null character.
questions.learningObjective: Allocate room for null terminators.

questions.title: fopen header
questions.prompt: Which header declares FILE and fopen?
questions.explanation: FILE and standard file I/O functions are declared in stdio.h.
questions.learningObjective: Include the correct header for file I/O.

questions.title: fopen failure
questions.prompt: What should you check after fopen?
choices: Whether the returned FILE object has length zero.
Whether fclose has already been called.
Whether the returned FILE * is NULL.
questions.explanation: fopen returns NULL when it cannot open the file.
questions.learningObjective: Handle file open errors.

questions.title: fclose responsibility
questions.prompt: Why should fclose be called on a successfully opened FILE *?
choices: To delete the file from disk.
To release the file resource and flush pending output.
questions.explanation: Closing files releases resources and ensures buffered output is written.
questions.learningObjective: Manage FILE resources correctly.

questions.title: fgets behavior
questions.prompt: What is true about fgets(buf, sizeof buf, fp)?
choices: It reads at most sizeof buf - 1 characters and null-terminates on success.
It returns the number of characters read as an int.
questions.explanation: fgets leaves room for '\0' and may keep the newline if there is space.
questions.learningObjective: Read lines safely with bounded input.

questions.title: scanf width
questions.prompt: Why is %9s safer than %s for char name[10]?
choices: It reads exactly 9 characters including spaces.
It limits input to 9 non-whitespace characters plus the null terminator.
It validates that input is alphabetic.
questions.explanation: A field width prevents writing past the fixed buffer.
questions.learningObjective: Use scanf widths for fixed-size string buffers.

questions.title: fread return value
questions.prompt: What does fread return?
choices: The number of complete items read.
questions.explanation: fread returns how many items, not bytes, were successfully read.
questions.learningObjective: Check binary I/O correctly.

questions.title: Binary versus text mode
questions.prompt: Why use "rb" when reading binary files portably?
choices: Binary mode makes the file encrypted.
Text mode may translate bytes such as newlines on some systems.
questions.explanation: On some platforms, text mode performs translations; binary mode requests raw bytes.
questions.learningObjective: Choose file modes intentionally.

questions.title: Ownership after malloc
questions.prompt: What does it mean when a function returns a malloc-allocated pointer to the caller?
choices: The caller usually becomes responsible for freeing it.
The pointer is automatically freed at the next semicolon.
The memory belongs to the compiler only.
The pointer can never be NULL.
questions.explanation: C has manual ownership conventions; returned allocated storage needs a clear owner.
questions.learningObjective: Track ownership responsibilities.

questions.title: Leak scenario
questions.prompt: What is the bug here if no other pointer stores the allocation?
choices: The second malloc appends to the first block.
The first allocation is leaked when p is overwritten.
p becomes a pointer to both allocations.
The compiler frees the first allocation automatically.
questions.explanation: Assigning a new allocation to the only pointer loses access to the old allocation.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize memory leaks from overwritten owning pointers.

questions.title: Freeing non-malloc memory
questions.prompt: Which pointer is valid to pass to free?
choices: The address of a local variable.
A pointer to the middle of an allocation.
A pointer returned by malloc/calloc/realloc that has not already been freed.
A pointer to a string literal.
questions.explanation: free must receive a null pointer or a pointer value returned by an allocation function.
questions.learningObjective: Call free only on valid owned allocations.

questions.title: Error cleanup path
questions.prompt: A function opens a file and then malloc fails. What should it do before returning an error?
choices: Ignore the file because malloc failed later.
Close the file it already opened.
questions.explanation: Cleanup should release resources acquired before the failure.
questions.learningObjective: Write reliable cleanup paths for multiple resources.

questions.title: Macro expansion hazard
questions.prompt: Why is this macro dangerous?
choices: Its parameters are not parenthesized, so precedence can change the result.
x is evaluated at compile time only.
questions.explanation: SQUARE(a + 1) expands to a + 1 * a + 1, not (a + 1) * (a + 1).
questions.learningObjective: Write safer expression macros.

questions.title: Macro double evaluation
questions.prompt: What is the issue with MIN(i++, j)?
choices: The ?: operator cannot be used in macros.
i++ may be evaluated more than once.
questions.explanation: Macro arguments are substituted textually, so an argument used twice can run twice.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid side-effecting expressions in unsafe macros.

questions.title: Include search form
questions.prompt: What is the usual difference between #include <stdio.h> and #include "mylib.h"?
choices: They are exactly identical on every compiler.
Quotes can include only binary files.
Angle brackets include the file twice.
Angle brackets search system include paths; quotes commonly search the local/project path first.
questions.explanation: Compilers commonly treat quoted includes as project/local headers before standard include paths.
questions.learningObjective: Use include syntax appropriately.

questions.title: #define constant
questions.prompt: What does the preprocessor do with #define SIZE 10?
choices: It replaces later SIZE tokens with 10 before compilation.
It creates a typed int variable.
It allocates an array named SIZE.
It changes the linker search path.
questions.explanation: Object-like macros perform token replacement during preprocessing.
questions.learningObjective: Understand basic macro substitution.

questions.title: Prefer const or enum
questions.prompt: Why might enum { SIZE = 10 }; be preferable to #define SIZE 10 for an integer constant?
choices: It gives a real named integer constant visible to the compiler.
questions.explanation: An enum constant participates in C's syntax and diagnostics more directly than a textual macro.
questions.learningObjective: Choose typed language constructs over macros when possible.

questions.title: Conditional compilation
questions.prompt: What does #ifdef DEBUG test?
choices: Whether a variable named DEBUG is nonzero.
Whether the macro DEBUG is defined.
questions.explanation: #ifdef checks macro definition status during preprocessing.
questions.learningObjective: Use conditional compilation correctly.

questions.title: Syntax error from missing semicolon
questions.prompt: A compiler reports an error on the second line. What is the likely cause?
choices: The second line must be in a header.
The missing semicolon after the first declaration.
questions.explanation: A missing semicolon often makes the next line look wrong to the parser.
questions.learningObjective: Debug syntax errors by checking the previous statement too.

questions.title: Implicit function declaration problem
questions.prompt: Why is calling a function without a visible declaration a serious problem in modern C?
choices: The compiler may not know the correct parameter and return types, and modern standards reject implicit declarations.
The linker cannot ever link declared functions.
The preprocessor turns the call into a macro.
questions.explanation: Visible prototypes are required for reliable type checking and are expected by modern C compilers.
questions.learningObjective: Include headers or declarations before calling functions.

questions.title: Warning value
questions.prompt: Why should warnings be treated seriously while learning C?
choices: They often point to real bugs such as type mismatches or missing returns.
Warnings mean the executable was not produced.
questions.explanation: C allows many risky constructs, so warnings are an important safety net.
questions.learningObjective: Use compiler diagnostics as feedback.

questions.title: Segmentation fault clue
questions.prompt: A program crashes at *p = 1. What is the first thing to inspect?
choices: Whether p points to valid writable storage.
questions.explanation: Crashes on dereference commonly come from null, uninitialized, dangling, or otherwise invalid pointers.
questions.learningObjective: Debug pointer crashes methodically.

questions.title: Compiler versus linker
questions.prompt: Which issue is usually found by the linker, not the compiler?
choices: A missing closing brace in a source file.
Using = instead of == in an if condition.
A declared external function has no definition in linked object files.
questions.explanation: The linker combines object files and resolves external symbols.
questions.learningObjective: Classify build errors by compilation phase.

questions.title: Header circular dependency
questions.prompt: What often helps when two struct types refer to each other by pointer across headers?
choices: Putting both .c files in the header.
questions.explanation: Forward declarations let headers mention pointer types without needing full struct definitions.
questions.learningObjective: Reduce header coupling with incomplete types.

questions.title: assert header
questions.prompt: Which header provides assert?
questions.explanation: assert is declared as a macro in assert.h.
questions.learningObjective: Use standard debugging support.

questions.title: assert purpose
questions.prompt: What is assert best used for?
choices: Handling all user input errors in production.
questions.explanation: assert documents and checks conditions that should never be false if the program logic is correct.
questions.learningObjective: Apply assertions appropriately.

questions.title: errno use
questions.prompt: When is errno meaningful?
choices: At any time as a global success flag.
After a library function reports failure in a way that documents errno use.
questions.explanation: errno should be checked after a function indicates failure and specifies errno behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Use errno without treating it as a universal status variable.

questions.title: printf format mismatch
questions.prompt: What is wrong here if x has type long?
choices: printf automatically reads the declared type of x.
questions.explanation: printf uses the format string to know the argument types. A mismatch has undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Match printf conversions to argument types.

questions.title: size_t format
questions.prompt: Which printf conversion is correct for size_t?
questions.explanation: %zu is the standard conversion for size_t.
questions.learningObjective: Print size_t values portably.

questions.title: Preprocessed output
questions.prompt: Why might you inspect preprocessed output?
choices: To run the program step by step.
To see what includes and macros expanded into before compilation.
questions.explanation: Preprocessed output reveals the source that the compiler proper sees after macro expansion and includes.
questions.learningObjective: Debug macro and include problems.

questions.title: Header guard shape
questions.prompt: Which pattern is a conventional include guard?
questions.explanation: The #ifndef/#define/#endif pattern prevents repeated header inclusion.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize include guard syntax.

questions.title: Debugging minimal example
questions.prompt: When a bug is confusing, why make a small reproducible example?
choices: It isolates the behavior and removes unrelated code.
It changes undefined behavior into defined behavior.
It guarantees the compiler has a bug.
questions.explanation: Smaller examples make it easier to identify the exact language rule or program mistake involved.
questions.learningObjective: Use reduction as a debugging technique.

quizzes.title: Function Pointers, Bitwise Operations, and Qualifiers

questions.title: Function pointer declaration
questions.prompt: Which declares fp as a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning int?
questions.explanation: Parentheses around *fp are required; otherwise the declaration would be a function returning int *.
questions.learningObjective: Read and write function pointer declarations.

questions.title: Calling through function pointer
questions.prompt: Which call is valid if fp points to a compatible function?
questions.explanation: A function pointer can be called with normal call syntax.
questions.learningObjective: Call functions through pointers.

questions.title: Callback parameter
questions.prompt: What does apply accept as its second parameter?
choices: A pointer to a function taking int and returning int.
questions.explanation: The parameter int (*fn)(int) is a function pointer.
questions.learningObjective: Use function pointers for callbacks.

questions.title: qsort comparator
questions.prompt: What must a qsort comparison function return?
choices: Negative, zero, or positive depending on ordering.
A pointer to the smaller element.
questions.explanation: qsort comparators return an int less than, equal to, or greater than zero.
questions.learningObjective: Understand standard callback contracts.

questions.title: Bitwise AND
questions.prompt: What is 0b1100 & 0b1010 in binary?
questions.explanation: Bitwise AND keeps a bit set only when both operands have that bit set.
questions.learningObjective: Apply bitwise AND.

questions.title: Bitwise OR
questions.prompt: What does flags |= MASK do?
choices: Clears the bits that are set in MASK.
Sets the bits that are set in MASK.
questions.explanation: OR assignment turns on mask bits while leaving other bits unchanged.
questions.learningObjective: Set flag bits with masks.

questions.title: Bitwise clear
questions.prompt: Which expression clears the bits in MASK from flags?
questions.explanation: ~MASK has zeros where MASK has ones; ANDing clears those bits.
questions.learningObjective: Clear flag bits with masks.

questions.title: Bitwise toggle
questions.prompt: Which operator is commonly used to toggle selected bits?
questions.explanation: XOR with 1 flips a bit; XOR with 0 leaves it unchanged.
questions.learningObjective: Use XOR for bit toggling.

questions.title: Left shift
questions.prompt: For unsigned int x = 1u; what is x << 3?
choices: Undefined because all shifts are undefined.
questions.explanation: Left shifting unsigned 1 by 3 positions produces 2^3.
questions.learningObjective: Use unsigned shifts for bit masks.

questions.title: Shift count rule
questions.prompt: What is wrong with shifting a 32-bit unsigned int by 32?
choices: It is allowed only for signed integers.
The shift count must be less than the width of the promoted left operand.
questions.explanation: A shift count equal to or greater than the type width has undefined behavior.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid invalid shift counts.

questions.title: Signed shift caution
questions.prompt: Why prefer unsigned types for bit manipulation?
choices: Signed overflow and some signed shift cases can be undefined or implementation-defined.
Unsigned types cannot overflow in any sense.
Signed types cannot use bitwise operators.
Unsigned types are always exactly 32 bits.
questions.explanation: Unsigned integer arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N, making it more predictable for bit work.
questions.learningObjective: Choose appropriate integer types for bit operations.

questions.title: const object
questions.prompt: What does const int n = 5; primarily promise?
choices: The program should not modify n through that lvalue.
n must be stored in ROM.
n has external linkage by default.
questions.explanation: const qualifies the object type and prevents assignment through that name.
questions.learningObjective: Use const for read-only intent.

questions.title: const API contract
questions.prompt: Why should strlen take const char * rather than char *?
choices: It makes strlen faster in all cases.
It means the pointer cannot be NULL.
It promises not to modify the characters and accepts string literals.
It makes the string length compile-time constant.
questions.explanation: const char * lets callers pass read-only character arrays because the function only reads them.
questions.learningObjective: Apply const to function interfaces.

questions.title: volatile purpose
questions.prompt: What is volatile mainly for?
choices: Preventing all compiler optimization in the program.
Objects that may change outside normal program flow, such as memory-mapped I/O.
questions.explanation: volatile tells the compiler that accesses are observable and should not be optimized away like ordinary memory.
questions.learningObjective: Understand the limited purpose of volatile.

questions.title: volatile is not atomic
questions.prompt: Which statement is true?
choices: volatile does not by itself make increments thread-safe.
volatile makes every access locked by the CPU.
volatile prevents data races in C.
volatile is the same as restrict.
questions.explanation: volatile is not a synchronization primitive. Thread safety needs atomics, locks, or another correct concurrency mechanism.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid misusing volatile for synchronization.

questions.title: restrict basics
questions.prompt: What does restrict on a pointer parameter express?
choices: For that pointer's lifetime, the object it points to is accessed only through that pointer or values based on it.
The pointed-to object cannot be modified.
The pointer has static storage duration.
questions.explanation: restrict is an aliasing promise that can enable optimization when used correctly.
questions.learningObjective: Understand the basic contract of restrict.

questions.title: restrict violation
questions.prompt: What is the problem with passing the same array for both restrict parameters if both are used to access it?
questions.codeSnippet: void add(int * restrict a, int * restrict b, size_t n);
choices: It causes an automatic deep copy.
It forces the compiler to disable all optimization.
It violates the no-alias promise and can produce undefined behavior.
questions.explanation: restrict requires the caller to honor the aliasing contract.
questions.learningObjective: Use restrict only when aliases are controlled.

questions.title: Bit test
questions.prompt: Which condition tests whether FLAG_READ is set in flags?
questions.explanation: AND with the mask leaves a nonzero result only if at least one selected bit is set.
questions.learningObjective: Test flags with bit masks.

questions.title: Function returning pointer to function
questions.prompt: Which spelling is clearest for a function get_op returning a binary operation pointer?
choices: typedef int (*Op)(int, int); Op get_op(char c);
questions.explanation: A typedef can make complex function pointer interfaces much easier to read.
questions.learningObjective: Use typedefs to simplify callback-heavy declarations.

questions.title: Bit fields caution
questions.prompt: Why are struct bit-fields not always ideal for serialized file or network formats?
choices: Layout details such as order and padding are implementation-defined.
questions.explanation: For external formats, explicit masks and shifts on fixed-width unsigned types are usually more portable.
questions.learningObjective: Understand portability limits of bit-fields.

quizzes.title: Undefined Behavior and C Semantic Traps

questions.title: Unsequenced modification
questions.prompt: What is true about this expression?
choices: It is invalid syntax and cannot compile.
It has undefined behavior because i is modified more than once without sequencing.
questions.explanation: The side effects of i++ and ++i on the same scalar object are unsequenced relative to each other.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid expressions with unsequenced side effects.

questions.title: Signed overflow
questions.prompt: What happens if INT_MAX + 1 is evaluated as signed int?
choices: It becomes an unsigned int automatically.
questions.explanation: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid relying on signed overflow.

questions.title: Unsigned wrap
questions.prompt: What is true about unsigned integer overflow?
choices: It is undefined just like signed overflow.
It wraps modulo one more than the maximum value.
It turns the value into a float.
questions.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N for an N-bit unsigned type.
questions.learningObjective: Use unsigned arithmetic with clear modulo expectations.

questions.title: Strict aliasing intuition
questions.prompt: Why is reading an int object through a float * generally unsafe?
choices: int objects are always larger than float objects.
It can violate effective type/aliasing rules and has undefined behavior.
The compiler automatically converts the object to float.
questions.explanation: C has rules about which lvalue types may access an object's stored value.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid invalid type punning through incompatible pointers.

questions.title: Use memcpy for representation copy
questions.prompt: What is a safer way to copy the bytes of an int into an unsigned char buffer?
choices: sprintf(buf, "%d", x) for all binary uses
questions.explanation: memcpy copies object representations without violating aliasing rules.
questions.learningObjective: Use byte-copy APIs for representation-level work.

questions.title: Out of bounds write
questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
choices: a[3] writes past the end of a.
Only char arrays can be indexed.
questions.explanation: int a[3] has valid indexes 0, 1, and 2.
questions.learningObjective: Catch out-of-bounds array access.

questions.title: Mismatched printf arguments
questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
choices: printf cannot print the same variable twice.
The format string expects two int arguments, but only one is provided.
questions.explanation: Variadic functions such as printf rely on the format string matching the provided arguments.
questions.learningObjective: Match variadic function arguments to their format strings.

questions.title: Dangling returned pointer
questions.prompt: Why is using the returned pointer invalid?
choices: It points to a string literal.
It points to an object whose lifetime ended when make returned.
It points to allocated memory that must be freed.
questions.explanation: Automatic local arrays cease to exist when their block exits.
questions.learningObjective: Recognize dangling pointers from returned local addresses.

questions.title: Modifying string literal
questions.prompt: Which rewrite makes this modification valid?
questions.explanation: An array initialized from a string literal is a modifiable local array if not const.
questions.learningObjective: Use modifiable storage when changing strings.

questions.title: Invalid free target
questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
choices: p does not point to the start of the allocated block returned by malloc.
The allocation is too small for int.
free cannot be used on char pointers.
questions.explanation: free must receive the original allocation pointer or NULL, not an interior pointer.
questions.learningObjective: Free exactly the allocation pointer you own.

questions.title: Reading beyond null terminator
questions.prompt: Why can strlen crash or run too far on this buffer?
choices: The array is not guaranteed to contain a null terminator.
strlen stops at newline, not null.
questions.explanation: strlen scans until it finds '\0'. Without one in bounds, it reads beyond the array.
questions.learningObjective: Provide null-terminated strings to string functions.

questions.title: Division by zero
questions.prompt: What happens when integer division by zero is evaluated?
choices: The compiler converts it to floating-point division.
questions.explanation: C does not define integer division by zero.
questions.learningObjective: Guard divisors before integer division or remainder.

questions.title: Null pointer dereference
questions.prompt: What is true about *p when p is NULL?
choices: It is allowed only in main.
questions.explanation: A null pointer does not point to an object.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid dereferencing null pointers.

questions.title: Effective type and unsigned char
questions.prompt: Which pointer type is specially allowed to inspect an object's bytes?
questions.explanation: Character types can access the object representation of any object.
questions.learningObjective: Know the safe byte-inspection exception.

questions.title: Sequence with comma operator
questions.prompt: Is this expression well-defined?
choices: No; all uses of ++ twice are undefined.
Yes; the comma operator sequences the left expression before the right.
No; comma in C never sequences.
questions.explanation: The comma operator introduces a sequence point between its left and right operands.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sequenced from unsequenced side effects.

questions.title: Order of function arguments
questions.prompt: Why is this call unsafe?
choices: i++ is illegal in function arguments.
The evaluations of function arguments are not sequenced relative to each other.
The comma between arguments is the comma operator.
questions.explanation: The order of evaluating function arguments is unspecified, and modifying i while also reading it unsequenced can be undefined.
questions.learningObjective: Avoid side effects that depend on argument evaluation order.

questions.title: Uninitialized pointer
questions.prompt: What should be done before this dereference?
choices: Assign p a valid address, such as &x or allocated storage.
questions.explanation: Declaring a pointer does not make it point anywhere valid.
questions.learningObjective: Initialize pointers before use.

questions.title: Lifetime of compound literal
questions.prompt: Inside a block, how long does a non-static compound literal object generally live?
choices: Until the end of the enclosing block.
questions.explanation: A compound literal at block scope has automatic storage duration.
questions.learningObjective: Reason about lifetimes of temporary-looking C objects.

questions.title: memcpy overlap
questions.prompt: What should be used when source and destination ranges may overlap?
questions.explanation: memcpy requires non-overlapping ranges. memmove handles overlap.
questions.learningObjective: Choose memory-copy functions correctly.

questions.title: Why undefined behavior matters
questions.prompt: Why is relying on undefined behavior especially dangerous?
choices: It always produces the same crash.
It is defined by the operating system only.
The compiler may assume it never happens and optimize in surprising ways.
It only affects comments and formatting.
questions.explanation: Undefined behavior gives the implementation no required semantics, so optimization can make bugs appear unrelated.
questions.learningObjective: Treat undefined behavior as a correctness issue, not a quirky result.
